Cardiovascular aging

A long-term study in accelerated-aging AC8 mice reported higher ejection fraction, lower aortic stiffness, improved gait symmetry, and higher survival than in untreated AC8 controls. Survival did not differ significantly in wild-type mice. Human relevance has not been tested.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A long-term study in accelerated-aging AC8 mice reported higher ejection fraction, lower aortic stiffness, improved gait symmetry, and higher survival than in untreated AC8 controls. Survival did not differ significantly in wild-type mice. Human relevance has not been tested.

Summary of the Evidence

One original animal study was identified for cardiovascular aging. It examined near-infrared PBM in an accelerated-aging transgenic mouse model and reported several cardiac, vascular, gait, and survival outcomes. There are no human or clinical studies in the indication set, and no separate in-vitro or ex-vivo experiment was identified. The result is a single-model signal rather than independent confirmation across laboratories or ordinary aging populations (Syed et al. 2023).

Human and clinical evidence

No study has tested PBM to prevent or treat cardiovascular aging in people. The mouse findings cannot establish whether the intervention affects human blood pressure, heart failure, cardiovascular events, physical function, or lifespan.

Animal evidence

Fourteen-month-old mice overexpressing adenylyl cyclase type VIII, a model of accelerated cardiac aging, and wild-type littermates received near-infrared exposure or served as controls. During the early treatment period, the authors reported reduced age-associated increases in left-ventricular mass, lower end-diastolic volume in AC8 mice, increased ejection fraction, reduced aortic-wall stiffness, and improved gait symmetry. After treatment was paused and then resumed, some effects persisted. Cumulative survival was reported as 100% in treated AC8 mice versus 43% in untreated AC8 controls. These outcomes come from one small, genetically specific experiment and do not establish extended human life or an effect on aging in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or tissue experiment was identified for this indication. The paper discusses TGF-β1 and other mechanisms, but measurements in treated mice are not a separate in-vitro demonstration of causation.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used 850 nm near-infrared light, which lies beyond visible red light, at a reported irradiance of 25 mW/cm² for two minutes on weekdays. The schedule lasted eight months, with treatment for 3.5 months, a three-month pause, and then 1.5 months of resumed exposure. The reported fluence was 3 J/cm². Because the paper itself calls for dose-optimization work, this schedule should be viewed as one experimental protocol, not an established optimum. Whole-body exposure in mice also differs from a targeted treatment in people, and the experiment does not identify which tissue mediated each outcome.

Interpretation

In the accelerated-aging AC8 mice, near-infrared exposure increased ejection fraction and gait symmetry, reduced aortic stiffness and several age-related cardiac changes, and was associated with higher survival: 100% versus 43% in untreated AC8 mice. Survival was not significantly improved in wild-type mice. This is a set of favorable outcomes in one long-term model study, not evidence that PBM slows ordinary aging or improves cardiovascular health in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for cardiovascular aging outcomes or survival
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One long-term experiment in accelerated-aging AC8 mice reported higher ejection fraction, lower aortic stiffness, improved gait symmetry, and higher survival than in untreated AC8 mice. Survival did not differ significantly in wild-type mice. These are favorable results in a specialized model, but one study cannot establish an effect in people. Independent models and dose studies should precede human testing.
